messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mai is a 57-year-old midwife, married for thirty years, who came to therapy six months after the rape that occurred late one evening in the hospital parking garage. She had just finished a difficult delivery and was walking to her car when a man she did not recognize grabbed her from behind. She remembers the burnt smell of the garage’s industrial exhaust fans mixing with his sweat. She did not scream; she went still, certain that if she fought, he would kill her. For weeks afterward, she told no one, not even her husband. She showered twice a day and scrubbed her skin until it was raw, trying to erase the sensation of his hands and the smell that clung to her hair.

In the months that followed, Mai found herself unable to walk through the hospital’s parking garage without her chest tightening and her palms slicking with sweat. She began arriving thirty minutes early for every shift so she could park in the furthest, most visible spot near the entrance, and she always kept her keys pressed between her fingers as she walked. She also started taking the stairs instead of the elevator, because the enclosed space made her feel trapped. At home, she became hypervigilant in ways that surprised even her. She listened for sounds that might mean someone was entering her home—the creak of a floorboard, the click of a lock—and she studied the faces of every man who walked past her in the grocery store, cataloging his posture, his gaze, the set of his jaw. What frightened her most was the way her body reacted before her mind caught up: a sudden racing heart, a wave of nausea, a tremor in her hands, all triggered by something as ordinary as the burnt smell of toast in the morning or the feeling of a stranger standing too close in line. She had come to believe that her own body was no longer trustworthy, that it would betray her with panic at any moment.

The burnt smell was the worst. It came from nowhere—a neighbor’s barbecue, a car exhaust, the hospital’s laundry room—and each time, she was back in that garage, her mind blank with terror. She began avoiding the hospital’s basement level entirely, asking colleagues to cover her deliveries if they required her to go near the garage entrance. Her supervisor noticed and expressed concern, but Mai could not explain. She was certain that if she told anyone, they would see her as weak or, worse, as someone who had invited the assault. She began to feel like a stranger in her own life, a woman who once had been calm and competent now jumping at shadows.

The cycle tightened. Every time she felt uncomfortable—a man’s eyes lingering a moment too long, the press of a crowd in the elevator—she would scan his face for threat, and her body would react with a surge of adrenaline, which confirmed that danger was real. This only made her more vigilant, more watchful, more afraid. She began to avoid social gatherings, claiming exhaustion, because being seen felt like being exposed. She stopped going to her weekly book club. Her husband noticed her withdrawing and asked if something was wrong, but she shook her head and turned away.

What finally brought Mai to therapy was a moment in the delivery room. A new father, excited and nervous, stepped too close to her as she handed him his baby. The burnt smell from the hospital’s incinerator drifted through an open window. Mai froze. Her hands shook so badly she nearly dropped the infant. She excused herself, went to the bathroom, and cried. That night, she told her husband the truth for the first time. He held her and said nothing, and the next morning he found her a therapist who specialized in trauma. Mai is terrified that she will never feel safe again, but she is also desperate to return to the work she loves without the constant fear that her own body will betray her.
